newsitem.title: USA: Clinton under pressure to name banker to Fed board.
newsitem.headline: Clinton under pressure to name banker to Fed board.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The Clinton administration is under pressure from the banking industry to nominate a banker to the Federal Reserve Board but the right person may be hard to find.

"We'll be pushing very, very hard to get a banker," Kenneth Guenther, Executive Vice President of the Independent Bankers Association, said. "They really need someone who knows the nuts and bolts of banking and banking regulation."
James Chessen, chief economist at the American Bankers Association, agreed.
"It's extremely important that there be someone on the board with a banking and financial industry background," Chessen said.
Fed sources said that central bank Chairman Alan Greenspan would also like to see a banker join the board.

Administration officials said they were still looking for the best candidates to fill the two Fed posts that will become vacant with the departure soon of the Lawrence Lindsey and Janet Yellen from the central bank board.

"We're working our way through the process of finding highly qualified people, but we're not there yet," Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said. "Certainly the right banker would be a very attractive candidate," he added.

But finding the right banker might be easier said than done. Not that many bankers are members of President Clinton's Democratic Party. And any banker who joins the Fed would have to sell off his or her holdings of bank shares, a disincentive to taking the job.
Administration officials said they tried to find a banker for the Fed last year who both qualified for, and wanted, the post.
But they were unable to entice anyone to take the job and instead ended up tapping White House Budget Director Alice Rivlin and private economist Laurence Meyer for the board.
Among bankers who were considered for the Fed at that time were former Wachovia Corp Chairman John Medlin and Anthony Terracciano, who had been with First Fidelity Bancorp.

The imminent departure from the Fed of Lindsey for a conservative think tank and Yellen for the White House as chief economist has given the administration another chance to find someone with banking expertise to join the Fed.

Among some of the new names that have surfaced as possible candidates are Joseph Bracewell, who heads Century National Bank here and who briefly served under Democratic President Jimmy Carter, and Douglas Harris, an African-American lawyer who was formerly with the Office of the Comptroller of Currency.
Administration officials have said they expect Clinton to try to fill at least one of the empty Fed positions with a woman or a member of a minority group.
Chessen, of the American Bankers Association, said the administration should also consider bank economists for the central bank board.

A wide range of possibilities have been mentioned, including James Annable of First Chicago NBD, Lynn Reaser of Jacksonville, Fla.,-based Barnett Banks Inc., Sung Won Sohn of Minneapolis's Norwest Corp., and John Wilson of California's Bank of America.

Federal law prevents the president from appointing more than one governor from any of the Fed's 12 districts and that could limit Clinton's choices. The Chicago, Dallas, New York Philadelphia and St. Louis districts are already represented.
That leaves Atlanta, Boston, Cleveland, Kansas City, Minneapolis, Richmond, Va. and San Francisco open.
The banking industry has been without representation on the seven-man Fed board since former banker John LaWare stepped down in April 1995.
The president's nominations to the Fed are subject to Senate confirmation.
